books.section: C. Reducing Big Government: Rhetoric and Reality
Reagan, H. W., Clinton, and W. (1980-2001)

stem: Which of the following best explains the change shown in the table?

options.text: Reagan raised taxes sharply while cutting military spending
options.misconception: Reagan cut taxes and raised military spending — the opposite of this choice.

options.text: Congress balanced the budget by eliminating Social Security and Medicare
options.misconception: Social Security and Medicare survived every attempt to cut them; they were never eliminated.

options.text: The economy collapsed, wiping out federal tax revenue entirely
options.misconception: The early-1980s recession was real, but tax revenue did not vanish — the debt grew because spending rose while revenue fell.

options.text: Tax cuts reduced federal revenue while military spending rose sharply

rationales.A: Background: Reagan cut taxes and raised military spending — the opposite of this choice.
rationales.B: Background: Social Security and Medicare survived every attempt to cut them; they were never eliminated.
rationales.C: Background: the early-1980s recession was real, but tax revenue did not vanish — the debt grew because spending rose while revenue fell.
rationales.D: Background: the 1981 tax cuts shrank federal revenue while the military buildup pushed spending up, so the government borrowed the difference.
rationales.general:
1. Read the table like a before-and-after picture. In six years the debt more than doubled.
2. Background: the 1981 tax cuts shrank what the government took in, while the military buildup pushed what it spent up.
3. Background: when spending rises and revenue falls at the same time, the gap has to be borrowed — and the debt grows.
4. The other choices get the history backwards: taxes were cut, not raised.
Remember: the debt doubled because money went out faster than it came in.
